newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala withheld intervening as quetzal weakened.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala withheld intervening as quetzal weakened.

text.p: Economic factors, rather than Central Bank manipulations or rampant speculation, influenced the weakening of the Guatemalan quetzal in January, the Central Bank said Friday.
"Up to now the Central Bank has not participated at all in the market because we believe there are economic reasons that have affected the trend," Central Bank President Willy Zapata told reporters.
Zapata said the bank was watching demand for dollars and could intervene if it saw a growing amount of speculation.
The quetzal gained strength throughout last year and traded around 5.98 to the dollar in the last days of 1996. Friday's bank rate for the quetzal versus the dollar was 6.09750/6.10931.
Zapata said three factors influenced the quetzal's depreciation during the first weeks of the year.
-- Short-term interest rates went down, generating funds transfers to the foreign exchange market and increasing the demand for dollars.
-- Importers increased their demand for dollars in January because they had held off importing late last year, anticipating lower import duties that took effect January 1.
Zapata said a gain of $47 million in international monetary reserves since January 1, for a total of $860 million, allowed a forecast of a stable exchange rate in the rest of the year.
Twice in late December, President Alvaro Arzu said Guatemala was concerned with the strength of its currency, which negatively affected the value of its exports.
Zapata said it was not a coincidence that a depreciation in the quetzal followed Arzu's remarks.
"Undoubtedly it is not a coincidence because the economic cabinet discusses these issues and the president is informed about these discussions," Zapata said.
But Zapata said the way the Central Bank has worked to fight true appreciation in the quetzal, and a loss of competitivity in exports, was to fight to keep inflation down.
Inflation through Jan. 24 was 0.53 percent in 1997 compared to 0.38 percent in the same period last year. Guatemalan consumer prices rose 10.85 percent in 1996, compared to 8.61 percent for 1995.
